opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the clearest places is anywhere people are already paying a lot of money for expert judgment and where being wrong is costly. So think about forecasting, finance, law, medicine, scientific research. There are enormous markets where the product is essentially "tell me what's true, and tell me how confident to be." If you can build AI systems that are reliably calibrated, that say "I'm 70% confident" and are right about 70% of the time, that's worth a great deal to a hedge fund, to a company making strategic decisions, to a government agency trying to anticipate events.

And forecasting is especially attractive because you get ground truth. Questions resolve. You can score a system's track record over thousands of predictions, so you can actually tell whether it's good, which is much harder for, say, an AI producing persuasive essays. That gives you a tight feedback loop for training and a clear way for customers to verify value. Things like prediction platforms, or internal forecasting at large firms, are natural early customers.

Beyond that, there's a broad demand for trustworthy research assistance: systems that can read the literature, check claims, find the strongest counterarguments, and show their work so a human can audit the reasoning. Businesses would pay for that just because bad information is so expensive.

The important caveat is that the commercial incentive isn't automatically aligned with truth. There's also a lot of money in telling people what they want to hear, in engagement, in flattery. So the opportunity I'm most excited about is the segment where customers really do bear the cost of being wrong, because there the market rewards accuracy rather than agreeableness. And if we build up those capabilities and that culture of measurable honesty early, it carries over to the more important uses later, like helping society and policymakers reason well about AI itself.

r001.rationale: The response says costly errors create demand for accuracy and that some customers reward truth, but it does not explain that hallucinations and errors limit AI systems’ economic usefulness or identify a commercial incentive for large AI companies to reduce them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most obvious one is forecasting, and more broadly anything where there's a crisp, checkable question with a lot of money riding on the answer. Finance is the extreme case. Hedge funds already pay enormous sums for marginal improvements in predicting prices or earnings or macro variables, and the feedback is brutal and fast: you either made money or you didn't. So there's a ready buyer for systems that are actually calibrated rather than merely persuasive.

But I'd generalise that. Any domain where you can score the output against reality has this property. Medical diagnosis and prognosis, where you eventually learn whether the patient had the condition. Litigation outcomes, where the case gets decided. Supply chain and demand forecasting, where the inventory either sold or it sat there. Insurance underwriting. In all of these, the thing a customer actually wants is a probability that's right, and they can measure whether they got it. That's very different from, say, chatbots giving general advice, where the user often can't tell a confident wrong answer from a correct one and so the commercial pressure pushes toward sounding good rather than being good.

What makes this interesting from my point of view is that the same machinery you'd build for a commercial forecasting product is the machinery you'd want for epistemic improvement generally. If you train systems on track records, on proper scoring rules, on calibration across thousands of resolved questions, you get something that can be held to account in a way human pundits never are. You can then ask it about questions that resolve further out, or questions where the stakes are political rather than financial, and you have some basis for trusting it because it has a measurable record on the things that did resolve.

So the sequence I'd expect is: the money shows up first in finance and in enterprise forecasting, that funds the development of genuinely calibrated systems, and then those systems get pointed at harder, less lucrative, but more socially important questions. The risk is that the second step doesn't happen on its own, because the incentive to be right about, say, the effects of a policy ten years out is much weaker than the incentive to be right about next quarter's numbers. That's where I think philanthropic and governmental effort should concentrate: building the evaluation infrastructure, the long-horizon question banks, the institutional willingness to actually defer to systems with demonstrated track records. The commercial part will largely take care of itself.

r001.rationale: The response connects commercial value to calibrated, accurate predictions and notes that users may not detect confident wrong advice. It does not state that hallucinations and errors limit AI systems’ economic usefulness or identify large AI companies as having an incentive to reduce them.

astra-6.text:
I think the most obvious opportunity is in cases where people have a lot of money riding on getting the answer right. If you’re making an investment decision, or deciding whether to undertake some expensive project, you’d like an AI that will tell you when your assumptions are wrong. A system that flatters you and confirms what you already believe can be quite costly in those settings.

And there’s an opportunity to sell verification as a separate service. Someone brings you an analysis, perhaps produced by another AI, and you ask: Are the factual claims correct? Does the evidence actually support the conclusion? What has been left out? The customer is paying you to find problems, so pointing out a mistake is a success rather than an unpleasant interaction.

That doesn’t mean market incentives reliably produce truth everywhere. People also pay for reassurance and for arguments that help them persuade others. But where there’s a reasonably clear connection between accurate beliefs and better decisions, there’s a strong commercial reason to build systems that help you get things right.

r001.rationale: The response says errors can be costly and describes commercial demand for accurate answers, but it does not explain that hallucinations limit AI systems’ economic usefulness or identify large AI companies’ incentive to reduce them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the clearest opportunities is helping people evaluate decisions where they have a lot of money at stake. If you're considering an investment, buying a business, or making a major purchase, you have a reason to pay for an accurate assessment, including information that might change your mind.

That's a different incentive from a system funded by advertising, where success might mean keeping you engaged or persuading you to buy something. You could have an AI that works for the buyer, looks critically at the seller's claims, and checks the evidence. And the buyer can pay quite a lot for that service if even a small improvement in the decision is valuable.

The complication is that being paid by the user doesn't automatically mean telling them the truth. Users can also reward flattery or reassurance. So I would expect this to work best initially in areas where you can check the answers and where mistakes have fairly clear costs.

r001.rationale: The response mentions checking evidence and the costs of mistakes, but does not explain that hallucinations and errors limit AI systems’ economic usefulness or that this gives large AI companies a commercial incentive to reduce them.
